records.text: The Specific Task screen is intended to let users manage a particular task and start annotation from its document list. The screen can show task name, task ID, description, tagger, checker, and due date; a table of documents with document name, document ID, status, tagger, and assigned date; and a Back to Task Management button.

Suggested document statuses for the Specific Task screen are Not Started, In Progress, Ready for Review, In Review, Complete, and Rejected. Suggested status colors are light gray, yellow, light green, dark green, blue, and red, respectively. Use of sufficient contrast was recommended so statuses remain easy to see, including for users with color blindness.

The Specific Task screen's goals include centralizing the documents assigned to a task, showing task details such as tagger, checker, assigned date, due date, and description, and supporting management of document statuses during annotation. Proposed features include viewing tagger and checker annotations and changing document statuses.

A proposed administrator use case has the administrator log in, open the Specific Task screen, select a task, and view its details and document list. The system displays an overall task progress bar and each document's tagging or checking status; the administrator can change a document's status through a status-field dropdown.

A proposed administrator use case for assigning a tagger is: open and select the task, choose Assign Tagger, select a tagger from the available taggers, and click Assign; the system updates the task information to show the assigned tagger.

A proposed administrator use case for assigning a checker is: open and select the task, choose Assign Checker, select a checker from the available checkers, and click Assign; the system updates the task information to show the assigned checker.

A proposed tagger use case is: log in, open an assigned task, choose a document from its list, and have the system open the annotation tool. The tagger annotates and saves the document; the proposed flow sets its status to Ready for Review.

A proposed checker use case is: log in, open an assigned task, choose a document, and review it in the annotation tool. The checker can approve the document, which sets its status to Complete, or reject it with comments, which sets its status to Rejected and allows the tagger to annotate it again.

Proposed acceptance criteria for the Specific Task screen are that its document list is accurate and up to date; task and assignment details are correct; status changes work and appear in the list; tagger and checker annotations are visible; and the screen is accessible from the main menu and easy to use.
The conversation concerns requirements and use cases for a Specific Task screen in an annotation-management system. No personal identities or pronoun mappings established.

In a court opinion concerning a contract for levee works for the Council of Brewarrina, the judge said the integrity of the entire levee system was important because seepage around culverts or loose fill and deep cracks could cause failure. Professor Fell, an expert witness for the Council, testified that even one poorly compacted soil layer could create a seepage path and initiate erosion.

The judge held that contractual testing requirements at culverts were intended to assure the Council of the work’s quality and the levee system’s integrity. A failure to conduct required tests did not automatically prove the completed work failed to substantially comply, but once that testing failure was established, Beckhaus had the evidentiary onus to provide equivalent assurance through later tests or other evidence.

The judge said Beckhaus’s failure to add 3% lime to all material raised a prima facie doubt about whether the levees had the qualities that the lime was intended to provide. The judge also found that the circumstances of the CETS compaction tests weakened the assurance their passing results otherwise would have supplied.

Although approximately 340 randomly located CETS compaction tests passed, some test locations were reworked with added lime after testers warned Beckhaus that the areas were likely to fail; an adjacent or nearby area was then retested. Mr Rudge described this practice, and the judge concluded it reduced the assurance provided by the passing results and reinforced the need for Beckhaus to rebut the inference arising from failure to provide required test results under clauses 3.8 and 8.9.3 of the specification.

The judge concluded that evidence of compaction actually being carried out at culverts, apparently using appropriate techniques, did not provide the same assurance as satisfactory tests performed at the frequency required by the contract. The judge held that the Master erred in finding substantial compliance with the contractual compaction requirements over culverts.

The judge held that the Council of Brewarrina was entitled to damages for breach of contract caused by the failure to conduct required compaction tests at culverts. The damages were to cover rectification costs, including removing fill over and around the culverts far enough to redo the work in accordance with the contract; assessment of damages was proposed to be remitted to Macready AsJ.
